item.title: Bavuma, Jansen lead South Africa fightback in second test
item.description: South Africa captain Temba Bavuma and all-rounder Marco Jansen led a record-breaking fightback to take their side to 216 runs for six wickets at lunch on the third day of the second test at St George's Park on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: South Africa captain Temba Bavuma and all-rounder Marco Jansen led a record-breaking fightback to take their side to 216 runs for six wickets at lunch on the third day of the second test at St George's Park on Tuesday. Bavuma was 76 not out after the first session in a gritty display while big-hitting Jansen scored 72 off 71 balls in an unbeaten 106-run seventh-wicket partnership as the home side clawed their way out of a precarious position. The partnership came off 133 balls and broke the previous South Africa record of 89 runs for the seventh wicket in a test at St George’s Park, set against England in 1896. South Africa resumed on 97-5 after only 43 overs were bowled on the opening two rain-affected days with Bavuma on 41 and Wiaan Mulder on two. Mulder was the only wicket to fall on Tuesday as he ducked into a short-pitched ball from Mitchell Starc and gloved the ball behind to slip Matt Renshaw. It was Starc’s 450th test wicket but was only given out after a review. Australia had to do without seamer Josh Hazlewood for the first session because he did not field on Monday after falling ill and was serving penalty time before being allowed to bowl. He will be able to do so after lunch with the new ball due eight overs into the afternoon session.

item.title: How (and why) we developed 'The Age of Heat Storms'
item.description: I have been writing about climate change and climate scientists for years, and I have been frustrated by a disconnect between scientists and the public that I’ve seen time and again. Scientists and researchers often discuss global warming in the context of risks that will arise if the planet’s average global temperature rises more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels. Scientists aside, what is an ordinary person to make of that? Not much, in my experience.
item.dc:creator: Maurice Tamman
item.content:encoded: I have been writing about climate change and climate scientists for years, and I have been frustrated by a disconnect between scientists and the public that I’ve seen time and again. Scientists and researchers often discuss global warming in the context of risks that will arise if the planet’s average global temperature rises more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels. Scientists aside, what is an ordinary person to make of that? Not much, in my experience. Another frustration: There is no shortage of stories predicting the dire consequences we face if we don’t find a way to stop the planet’s temperature from rising beyond that threshold. But what about now? What has already happened? And why do these dire warnings so often land with a shrug? So I asked myself, “How do most people interact with weather and temperatures?” They get up in the morning and wonder how hot and how cold it will be. No one asks themselves, “What will the average temperature be today?” And when they wake up on the seventh day of a summer heat wave, they might groan and ask, “Will this ever end?” They might also lament that there have been several such heat waves this year, more than they remember growing up. Heat waves, it seemed to me, are the connective tissue between the science of global warming and our everyday experience. Heat waves are something people already understand, and I thought perhaps they could help explain how much the planet has warmed in recent decades. Unfortunately, no universally accepted definition of a heat wave existed. So, in consultation with climate researchers, a few of us at Reuters set out to build our own. Data journalists Ben Welsh, Charles Szymanski and I started seriously thinking about this idea in 2024, and this year Welsh rolled out the Reuters Climate Monitor , which tracks daily anomalous temperatures worldwide. Under the hood of the Climate Monitor, however, was a more ambitious system of concepts and methods we developed to define, track and map heat waves. The fact that heat waves have become more frequent and larger didn’t surprise me – but what our data analysis turned up is breathtaking and ominous. One thing we discovered is that we needed a new term for the largest heat waves, something simple that would instantly convey their scale and consequences. So we created a new category, the “heat storm” — defined as heat waves that at their peak cover at least 1% of the planet, about half the size of Canada. Some scientists objected to the term, because “storm” has a distinct meteorological definition. But it also has a common metaphorical meaning — “ a serious disturbance of any element of nature ,” per Merriam-Webster — that we believe fits these heat events. The stories in our series, which you can read here , and our heat-storm tracking system rest on the methods and definitions below. We have also open-sourced our heat wave-tracking approach so others can conduct their own research on heat waves using a uniform definition. It can be found on our GitHub page . We consulted two dozen researchers and scientists for this project. Four of them were particularly influential as we developed our methodology. Alistair Hobday , of CSIRO, of Australia’s National Science Agency, for his work on marine heat waves; Lukas Brunner , at the University of Hamburg, who helped with our seasonal adjustments and baseline temperature ranges; Claudio Piani at the American University of Paris, who also helped us develop our historical temperature ranges; and Ed Hawkins at the University of Reading, who convinced us that this was not a fool’s errand. The detailed section below on Sources, Definitions and Methodology is aimed at climate and weather specialists, and it’s technical in places. For general readers, here are the essentials: We have created a universal definition of a heat wave in consultation with climate scientists, meteorologists and weather researchers. We did this by analyzing temperatures since the 1960s for more than one million grid squares covering the entire globe. Our process starts with determining the historical temperature range for each day of the year from 1961 to 1990 for each of the 1.04 million grid squares on the planet. A heat wave occurs when the daily high temperature for any location reaches at least the 90th percentile of the 1961-1990 historical range – in other words, the hottest 10% – for five days in a row. To measure the geographical extent of heat waves, we map neighboring heat wave grid squares that form a cohesive area. Because very large heat waves have a dramatically outsized effect on people, plants and animals, we created a further definition: If at any point a heat wave covers 1% of the planet, we designate it a “heat storm” and give it a name, as is done with tropical storms and hurricanes. Our temperature data comes from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. SOURCES, DEFINITIONS AND METHODOLOGY DATA SOURCE ERA5, 0.25 degrees, European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). This dataset incorporates a variety of climate data sources, including weather stations, satellites, weather balloons, and ship readings. It then feeds the data into a model that estimates temperature values for 1.04 million grid squares covering the planet. It is widely considered the gold standard of global climate data. (For full citation, please see below.) HISTORICAL (OR BASELINE) TEMPERATURES 1/1/1961-12/31/1990, using UTC dates with 24 hourly temperatures each day. SOURCE DATA POINTS The estimated average daily high and low air temperatures at two meters above the ground or water surface for each of the grid squares on the planet. TEMPERATURE THRESHOLDS FOR AN ANOMALY High temperature threshold: 90th percentile. Low temperature threshold: 10th percentile. TEMPERATURE DAILY SMOOTHING “Smoothing” aims to reduce the effect of one or two unusually hot or cold days over the 30-year baseline for any given calendar day. So, for each calendar date, the Reuters baseline temperature distribution consists of 930 values: the corresponding high/low observations from that date and the 15 calendar days before and after it across the 30-year baseline period. We calculate the 90th and 10th percentile thresholds from those values. In non-leap years, we generate synthetic Feb. 29 data by averaging Feb. 28 and March 1. SEASONAL ADJUSTMENT Because seasonal changes can creep into the edges of our 31-day window and skew the temperature distribution, we adjust our data using the method outlined in “ Pitfalls in diagnosing temperature extremes ,” a 2024 Nature Communications paper by Lukas Brunner of the University of Hamburg and Aiko Voigt of the University of Vienna. This is done by subtracting each calendar date’s 31-day average from the corresponding baseline value and then recalculating the distribution. We use that distribution, which we call the baseline range or historical range, to establish the percentile thresholds that define what qualifies as extreme. Brunner vetted the computer code implementing the seasonal adjustment technique. GRID SQUARE AREA A 0.25-degree grid covers about 770 km² (28 km × 28 km) in the tropics, 540 km² (28 km × 19 km) in the mid-latitudes, and 260 km² (28 km × 9 km) in the polar regions. AREA OF THE EARTH 5,100,720 km² 90TH/10TH PERCENTILE The 90th percentile represents the deviation from the historical norm that 9 out of 10 days would fall below – the threshold beyond which a day’s temperature is unusually warm for that calendar date in that grid square. The 10th percentile represents the deviation from the norm that 9 out of 10 days would exceed – the threshold below which a day’s temperature is unusually cool. We calculate these thresholds from seasonally adjusted baseline temperatures. We chose the 90th and 10th percentiles based on published research and consultations with climate and marine heat wave researchers. HEAT WAVE DEFINITION We identify a heat wave when a grid cell records five days with a weighted-average percentile rank at or above the 90th percentile. We did this so that slight dips below the 90th percentile on any given day don’t override the broader, obvious trend. The weighted average is calculated over a rolling 5-day window with exponential decay (factor 0.9). The decay favors temperatures on more recent days, so temperatures above the 90th percentile on day five can sometimes overcome temperatures slightly below the 90th percentile on day one or two, for example. We apply a one-day grace period throughout, meaning a cell may fail to qualify for a single day without ending the streak. Once the grace day for a grid cell is reset, it can be reapplied the day after the cell is reintegrated. Once five qualifying days are reached, the heat wave remains active as long as the weighted average percentile rank stays at or above the 90th percentile, subject to the same grace period. The Reuters technique adapts the definition of marine heat waves established in the 2016 paper " A hierarchical approach to defining marine heat waves " by Alistair Hobday of CSIRO and his coauthors. COLD SNAP DEFINITION A cold snap is identified when a grid cell records five days with a weighted average percentile rank at or below the 10th percentile. The weighted average is calculated over a rolling 5-day window with exponential decay (factor 0.9). A one-day grace period is applied throughout, meaning a cell may fail to qualify for a single day without ending the streak. Once five qualifying days are reached, the cold snap remains active as long as the weighted average percentile rank stays at or below the 10th percentile, subject to the same grace period. GRACE DAYS After entering into a heat wave or cold snap state, a grid cell can remain in that state if the cell drops below/above the 90th/10th percentile for one day but rises above/below the 90th/10th percentile the following day. The grace day acknowledges that small shifts in local temperatures for one day could break the continuity of a heat wave in a way that anyone living through it might dispute. We do not use grace day cells when calculating the area of a heat wave or heat storm, and we ignore them when deciding whether a place is inside a heat wave or heat storm on any given day. GEOMETRIES There are three geometries for heat waves and cold snaps. They are the actual geometry of the extreme weather event, which is the extent based on the grid squares in a state of heat wave or cold snap; the buffer geometry, which is used to join grid squares that are extremely close to each other but don’t touch into a common temperature event; and the grace geometries, which are used to track grace days. HEAT WAVE OR COLD SNAP EXTENT Generally, we merge all grid cells that are in the state of a heat wave or cold snap and that share an edge into a unified geometry. If two distinct areas are separated by just one grid square, we consider them the same heat wave or cold snap event. The event is declared on the first day it qualifies (the fifth day of abnormal heat or cold) and is assigned a unique ID. TEMPERATURE STORM A heat storm or cold storm is a heat wave or cold snap whose geometry reaches at least 1% of Earth’s area, approximately 5.1 million km². This threshold was somewhat arbitrary, but is meant to capture very large and rare heat wave and cold snap events. PERSISTENCE OF HEAT WAVES, COLD SNAPS AND TEMPERATURE STORMS If a buffer geometry from today overlaps at least 60% of a buffer geometry from the previous day, it inherits that storm ID. If it overlaps several buffer geometries from the previous day at the 60% threshold, it will inherit the storm ID of the buffer geometry with the largest area of overlap. If it does not meet the 60% threshold, it will generate a new storm ID. Over time, this process can cause storms to split, merge, or be created. NAMING STORMS A name is assigned on the first day the geometry reaches 1% of Earth’s total surface area. NAMES Using https://github.com/philipperemy/name-dataset , we pulled the most popular names by gender for each country, scored them by rank and aggregated them by continent so names common across multiple countries within a region score higher. We grouped them into 13-letter buckets for alphabetic balance, then organized them by continent and gender to ensure global representation. We removed obvious duplicates, names with fewer than three letters, and names with ambiguous or inappropriate English meanings. From an initial list of 4,000 names, we ended up with 2,380. An algorithm names each storm using a formula that ensures storms get names from different parts of the alphabet and different world regions, with alternating genders. The name is paired with the storm’s start year to create the final identifier. Our name database is available here . DETERMINING IF A CITY IS WITHIN A WAVE OR STORM We build a 3-by-3 grid centered on the grid square where the city center lies. If any part of that grid is within the actual geometry, the city is considered to be within the heat wave, cold snap or storm. In the tropics, it typically means the area must be within about 59 km of the city; in the mid-latitudes, about 51 km; and in the polar regions, about 44 km. In rare cases, this method may place a city in two or more temperature events at the same time. In such cases, we assign the city-day to the named heat storm if one exists; otherwise, we assign it to the event that started earliest globally. We count each calendar day only once, regardless of how many events overlap. COUNTING HEAT WAVE/COLD SNAPS AND STORM DAYS FOR A SPECIFIC PLACE Given that waves and storms must have been above or below the 90th or 10th percentile for five days before the start of the event, days that a city or other specific location has been in a heat wave are counted starting four days before the start date of the heat wave or cold snap. In other words, days are counted from when temperatures first become anomalous and later become a heat wave, cold snap or a storm. If a temperature event immediately precedes another temperature event, causing the events to overlap in days, we assign the four lead-in days to the larger event. So, if one event is a heat wave and the other is a heat storm, the lead-in days are categorized as heat storm days. TEMPERATURES FOR A PLACE OR SPOT ON THE PLANET INSIDE A TEMPERATURE EVENT Temperatures are taken using the 3-by-3 grid, but only the grid cells inside the event are used and then averaged. HISTORICAL TEMPERATURE RANGE FOR A PLACE OR SPOT ON THE PLANET For a specific place or spot on the planet, we calculate the average for the historical norm, the 90th percentile temperature and the 10th percentile temperature across the nine grid squares that comprise the 3-by-3 grid. HEAT WAVE INTENSITY LEVELS Grid squares are assigned an intensity level based on how much any day’s temperature exceeds the 90th percentile threshold. The level is determined by the ratio of the actual anomaly to the threshold gap. So if the baseline – or historical norm – is 25 C and the 90th percentile is 30 C, the threshold gap is 5 degrees. (For readers accustomed to Fahrenheit, 30 C is 86 F.) A high of 30 C would be 5 degrees above baseline, making it a level 1 day. A high of 35 C would be 10 degrees above baseline, or twice the threshold gap, making it a level 2 day. A high of 40 C (15 degrees above baseline, three times the gap) would be level 3; 45 C (20 degrees above baseline, four times the gap) would be level 4, and so on. Contiguous grid cells reaching the same intensity level are aggregated to create a geometry for that level within the storm. HEAT STORM CASCADES We define a cascade as heat storms that run consecutively or simultaneously for an uninterrupted period of time. The duration of a cascade is the number of days that at least one heat storm was active on the planet. KNOWN LIMITATIONS The ECMWF bases its entire system on a gridded dataset that is only as granular as each grid cell, which range in area from 260 km² in the polar regions to 770 km² in the tropics. The dataset’s temperature estimates are not actual observations but are modeled from observations, as the ECMWF explains here . The models can diverge notably from observations in complex terrain, such as high altitudes and coastal areas. For example, parts of New York City touch the Atlantic Ocean, and the temperature difference between a grid square partially covered by water and land and a grid square fully over land can be several degrees. Using a 3-by-3 grid around a particular place is one way Reuters attempts to minimize those limitations. Seasonal adjustment is another. item.title: Sterling rises as strong labour market data reinforces rate hike bets
item.description: The British pound rose on Tuesday after jobs data pointed towards a bottoming in the labour market, reinforcing the case for a rate hike from the Bank of England when it meets next month.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Indyk
item.content:encoded: The British pound rose on Tuesday after jobs data pointed towards a bottoming in the [USN:L8N46608R TEXT:"labour market"], reinforcing the case for a rate hike from the Bank of England when it meets next month. A preliminary measure of payrolled employees rose, the unemployment rate fell and average hourly earnings grew faster than expected in the three months to August, official figures showed. The labour market figures were the latest in a string of better-than-forecast economic data that could allow the BoE to raise rates at next month's meeting. "The UK economy is surprising on the upside. There's room for more hiking," said Tommy von Brömsen, FX strategist at Handelsbanken. "Rate differentials are going to go in favour of the pound going forward." Sterling was last up 0.3% against the dollar at $1.3343. Against the euro, the pound was also up 0.3% at 84.04 pence. It hit its strongest level against the single currency since May 2025 on Monday at 83.95 pence. BOE TO HIKE NEXT MONTH Money market futures were almost fully pricing in a quarter-point rate hike when the BoE announces policy on November 5. Investors were also fully pricing in four rate hikes by the middle of next year. Lloyds' senior UK economist Nikesh Sawjani believes some of the underlying metrics in Tuesday's labour market data do not strengthen the case for more rate rises from the BoE, notably a decline in vacancies which suggests subdued labour demand. "The release reinforces expectations of a November hike, rather than making a compelling case in itself for a more aggressive path thereafter," Sawjani said, adding that labour market developments remain secondary to the wider monetary policy narrative. "The outlook for bank rate continues to hinge primarily on developments in the Middle East, their implications for energy prices and whether higher costs generate second-round effects in domestic wages and prices." Oil prices were up sharply on Tuesday on few signs of progress in efforts to end the Middle East war. Brent crude futures were last above $111 per barrel, their highest since May.

item.title: Giant ‘heat storms’ are scorching the Earth. This is the story of the biggest one on record
item.description: In less than a lifetime, about six and a half decades, heat waves have evolved from sporadic, isolated episodes to massive, cascading weather events that can blanket vast swaths of the planet for months or even years at a time.
item.dc:creator: Maurice Tamman, Ben Welsh, Pete McKenzie, Charlie Szymanski, Delgerzaya Delgerjargal, Robbie Corey-Boulet, Loucoumane Coulibaly, Jeff Horwitz, Joan Faus
item.content:encoded:
In less than a lifetime, about six and a half decades, heat waves have evolved from sporadic, isolated episodes to massive, cascading weather events that can blanket vast swaths of the planet for months or even years at a time. The largest heat wave of the 1960s reached about 6% of the planet as it drifted for 46 days over the Atlantic Ocean, parts of Latin America and West Africa. The largest one this decade swept across almost 85% of the globe during its 367-day lifetime, stretching into the polar latitudes and touching virtually every human being on Earth. To continue calling such sprawling phenomena “heat waves” would be like calling a monsoon a rain shower. To understand the new reality of these immense expanses of heat, Reuters consulted with two dozen meteorologists and climate researchers – and analyzed temperatures for every hour of every day since 1960 for more than one million grid squares covering the entire globe. Out of those results we developed a new concept: the “heat storm.” Simply put, heat storms are supersized heat waves. Reuters uses a conservative benchmark to define an ordinary heat wave: five or more consecutive days of abnormally high temperatures. Then we define the largest heat waves – those that at their peak cover at least 1% of the globe, roughly half the size of Canada – as heat storms. Applying this definition, Reuters identified a startling transformation. Heat storms were rare in the 1960s, when they averaged about five active storms per year. This decade, heat storms have swarmed the planet, averaging about 102 a year. One of them caused this summer’s deadly heat in Europe, notching the highest June temperatures ever recorded in Bordeaux, Budapest, and Bilbao, the latter of which hit 42.7 degrees Celsius (108.9 degrees Fahrenheit). Roasting Europe for most of June and July, the heat storm warped steel railroad tracks, drove what European governments estimated were more than 10,000 excess [USN:L6N43C0MP TEXT:"deaths"] in a single week, and prompted Belgian zookeepers to cool their [USN:KCN1UJ25K TEXT:"tigers"] by feeding them raw meat encased in ice. The largest heat storm on record – the one that lasted for 367 days over 2023-2024 and reached almost 85% of the globe – sent temperatures in parts of the Philippines up to 38 C (100.5 F), immiserating students in the country’s mostly unairconditioned schools. In Manila, math teacher Joel Arrojado recalled a student who was face-down at his desk, crying. When Arrojado coaxed the boy into looking up, Arrojado saw his face and chest covered in blood. The boy, Arrojado said, had suffered a spontaneous nosebleed, a common problem in extreme heat. As more blood pumped from his nostrils, Arrojado recalled, the child pleaded with Arrojado to call his mother. As the same heat storm encased southern Louisiana for months, it exacerbated a historic drought.The state burned , suffering what the governor called “theworst wildfire we’ve seen since at least the Second World War” – and close to 600 other fires in August alone. Two months later, smoke from a smoldering marsh fire developed into a blinding “[USN:L1N3BU02R TEXT:"super fog"]” that caused a highway pile-up of at least 158 cars, killing seven people. The same heat storm helped fuel a 2023 Mediterranean cyclone that dropped massive rains over Libya. In the dead of night, two dams burst near the coastal town of Derna, washing away entire neighborhoods. A week later, on her hands and knees, [USN:L1N3AU0I9 TEXT:"Sabreen Blil clawed with her bare hands"] at the rubble of her brother’s house, hoping to dig out the dead. As she wept, she recited their names. “Taym, Yazan, Luqman, Salmah, Tumador, Hakim and his wife. Oh my God. My family, where are you?” she wailed. “Oh God. Even just one – my God – just let me find even one body.” During the annual Hajj pilgrimage in Saudi Arabia, the heat storm drove temperatures at Mecca’s Grand Mosque to 51.8 C (125.2 F), killing more than 1,300 pilgrims. Bodies [USN:L8N3II0KI TEXT:" lay"] in the streets. And as Europe’s largest recorded fire spread in Greece during the span of that same heat storm, the inferno killed migrants traversing the thick Dadia forest. Their corpses remained in the woods for days; even the vultures that might have fed on the bodies had fled the flames. These far-flung and seemingly unrelated catastrophes all shared a common connection: one single heat storm. Heat storms inflict “a major disruption to global civilization,” said James Renwick, professor of physical geography at New Zealand’s Victoria University of Wellington. “Heat is the biggest killer from climate change,” he said, noting that it can lead to “famine, hunger, death, conflict over resources.” A NEW WAY TO UNDERSTAND CLIMATE CHANGE Heat storms constitute a new way to conceptualize how Earth’s climate is changing as humanity pumps greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. The determination by climatologists that the average global temperature in 2025 was 1.47 C (2.6 F) above the pre-industrial level is useful to scientists and policymakers, but to many people it’s so abstract as to be meaningless. What people do understand are heat waves – in Spanish, an “ola de calor”; in Arabic, a “mawjat hararia”; in Mandarin, a “rè làng.” Yet no universal definition of a heat wave exists. For example, authorities differ over duration: The US National Weather Service defines a heat wave as “abnormally and uncomfortably hot” weather typically lasting “two or more days,” while the meteorological agencies of Australia , France , Spain and the United Kingdom set the threshold at three days. Some of those countries also have different rules for what temperatures qualify as a heat wave. Moreover, what constitutes a heat wave in Anchorage, Alaska, would not be considered a heat wave in Kuwait City. The climate in those places differs sharply, and a heat wave is an unusual period of hot weather for a particular place. Such dueling definitions made it all but impossible to gauge whether heat waves are more common globally now than in the past. But the system Reuters has devised delivers the precision needed to do so. We began by determining the historical temperature range for each day of the year from 1961 to 1990 for each of 1.04 million grid squares around the globe. The temperature data comes from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts , and our detailed methodology is here . A heat wave occurs when the daily high temperature for any location reaches at least the 90th percentile of the historical range – in other words, the hottest 10% – for five days in a row. So a July heat wave in Istanbul is five or more consecutive days of at least 25.6 C (78.1 F), whereas one in Phoenix, Arizona, needs to reach 40.3 C (104.5 F). In Reuters’ definition, a heat wave can happen in any season, so in Istanbul a January heat wave would be five consecutive days of at least (11.2 C) (52.2 F), and in Phoenix the threshold would be 20.8 C (69.4 F). To measure the geographical extent of heat waves, we map neighboring heat wave grid squares that form a cohesive area. Because very large heat waves exert an expanding effect on the planet’s rising temperatures, Reuters created a further definition: If at any point a heat wave covers 1% of the planet, we designate it a heat storm and give it a name, as is done with tropical storms and hurricanes. Naming events is “a powerful way for people to understand that something is happening,” Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, told Reuters. Yet “we don’t currently do that with heat waves,” he said, even though heat has been estimated to kill almost half a million people a year. Defining and naming heat storms is an important innovation, he added, and could help people to track impacts and consequences. As their numbers have swelled over the decades, heat storms and heat waves have not only caused individual catastrophes. They have also helped drive lasting, systemic effects. They exacerbate droughts and intensify fires – from Chile to Europe, the largest conflagrations on record happened during heat storms — and if they hit while a woman is pregnant, studies have found that she’s more likely to suffer everything from stillbirth to preeclampsia, a leading killer of expecting and post-partum women. Warmer temperatures can usher in benefits, at least for some regions. Siberia now produces almost as much wheat as Russia’s traditional breadbasket near the Black Sea. That’s in part because increasing heat storms and heat waves have helped open far northern latitudes to agriculture while simultaneously contributing to droughts around the Black Sea that reduce production there. 18 YEARS OF CONSTANT HEAT STORMS Tens of thousands of ordinary heat waves flicker in and out of existence every year. Like heat storms, they too have escalated in number, more than doubling from the 1960s to this decade. The vast majority are small, however, never even covering 0.01% of the planet, about the size of a square that you could drive across in less than two and a half hours. Only a minuscule fraction of heat waves ever gets big enough to become heat storms, which currently number about 102 annually. Yet heat storms now claim the lion’s share of Earth’s unusually hot days, those in the top tenth of the historical range. In the 1960s, heat storms averaged 3% a year for any given spot on the planet. (The remainder comprised ordinary heatwaves and short bursts of heat that didn’t last long enough to become a heatwave.) This decade, heat storms have accounted for almost 43% of such days. As greenhouse gas emissions have increased, so too have heat storms and ordinary heat waves. From the 1960s to this decade, the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has increased by more than 30%. Over that time, the average portion of the planet likely to be covered by heat storms and heat waves has risen more than 12-fold. El Niño – the periodic episodes of unusually warm water in the Pacific Ocean that drive major weather patterns – has acted as an accelerant, intensifying heat storms and heat waves. Reuters has also examined the opposite of heat waves and heat storms – cold snaps and cold storms. They have dwindled. From the 1960s to this decade, the total area in a cold snap or cold storm on an average winter day has shrunk by almost 80%. Despite their mammoth scale, the phenomenon of heat storms has been largely invisible to the public. Until recent decades, heat storms were rarer and smaller, so easier to overlook. But perhaps as importantly, they hadn’t been defined and named in the sharp way that typhoons and hurricanes are. Yes, people in Montreal, Perth and Hong Kong knew they were baking in a stretch of hot days – but they did not know that they were all experiencing one unitary heat storm. As part of this series examining heat storms and their effects, Reuters has integrated an online Heat Storm Tracker into our regular weather coverage. With this tool, people can see what had previously gone unnoticed and, using that knowledge, tally the impact of heat storms as they rage across regions. The rapid evolution of heat has not only made individual heat storms larger. Now, in sharp contrast to even 20 years ago, massive heat storms often run into, merge with, and split off from one another. What has become common are heat storms that run consecutively, simultaneously or both – heat storm cascades. The duration of these cascades swelled from an average of roughly two months in the 1960s to nine months in the first part of the 2000s. Then, on July 6, 2008, a cascade started – and has not stopped. For more than 18 years straight, 6,681 days, at least one heat storm has been roiling the planet, and often more than one. Many of them have been colossal. In the almost half century between 1960 and the start of the current 18-year cascade, only five heat storms had ever reached a peak size bigger than a tenth of the planet, about the area of Europe and Asia combined. The ongoing cascade has included 56 such mega heat storms. The largest of these was one we have named Heat Storm Vera, the storm that killed the Hajj pilgrims, intensified the Louisiana wildfires, and touched nearly 85% of the planet over its 367-day lifespan. What follows is a biography of Vera, from its birth on July 29, 2023, through its last day on July 29, 2024, that shows how the storm connected and often devastated communities scattered across the globe. TEXAS, AUGUST 2023: FRIDAY NIGHT LIGHTS On a sweltering evening in August 2023, as Heat Storm Vera coiled around the American South, Justice Trumpler led his high school football team onto the field for the season’s first game. In hopes of playing college ball, the 17-year-old captain had invited coaches and recruiters to watch. As the game kicked off at 7:30pm, the temperature was 37.8 C (100 F). Texas’s passion for high school football – the American version, not the one that transfixed billions during this summer’s World Cup – was captured in the iconic movie Friday Night Lights, about a team gunning for the state championship. But players of American football suffer 11 times as many heat-related injuries as athletes in all other sports combined, according to data from the University of Connecticut Korey Stringer Institute. That’s because the football season starts in the summer, the sport demands intense physical exertion, and many of its players, such as the 255-pound offensive lineman Trumpler, have large bodies that are harder to cool down. There’s another reason: In contrast to most other warm-weather sports, American football features heat-trapping helmets and heavy padding. Meanwhile, Texas is spending ever more time in extreme heat. Across the entire three decades from 1960 to 1989, the city of Austin – home to Trumpler’s Bowie High School – experienced a total of 557 days in heat waves and heat storms. This decade, our analysis shows, that number has already surpassed 700. During the football season, Heat Storm Vera enveloped Austin for 39 days. By halftime, the Bowie Bulldogs led 14-0. As the teams broke apart, Trumpler’s parents said they watched him walk to the field’s edge and vomit. A trainer hosed it away. Through the second half, they saw Trumpler stop to dry heave at least twice, they said, and he seemed slow to get off the turf after plays. At one point, his parents saw him walk toward the opposing team’s huddle, a sign of mental confusion. Trumpler’s father, Jason Trumpler, told Reuters he began shouting from the bleachers for the coaches to pull his son out of the game. When that didn’t work, he went to the railing separating the stands from the field and continued yelling. Trumpler kept playing. Bowie’s coach did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The school’s principal referred Reuters to a school district spokesman, who did not respond to messages seeking comment. Other players struggled, too. So many boys fell to the ground after plays that Bowie’s game commentators declared it a “cramp epidemic.” By the fourth quarter, the score was tied. The coaches could have ended the game, but the referee announced it would go into overtime. “Both teams are going to start on the 25 (yard line) of their opposition and, uh, keep on going until somebody dies,” said one commentator. “Don’t say that,” replied the other. The “unfortunate” phrasing, the first commentator told Reuters, was intended to convey how hard the teams were playing under very tough conditions. Just before the second-to-last play, a leg cramp brought Trumpler to the ground. His coach finally pulled him out. “Texas has that mentality of ‘you gotta be tough, you gotta play through pain,’” said Jason. Jason took Trumpler home, but the teen couldn’t stop throwing up. After an ice bath failed to cool Trumpler down, Jason said, he drove his son to the hospital. When Trumpler’s mother, Jennifer Norman-Wolfe, arrived, he couldn’t recognize her voice, she said, and couldn’t tell her how many brothers he had. Reuters was not able to review Trumpler’s medical records, but his parents said tests showed their son’s kidneys were failing, and his brain was swelling so much that doctors said they might need to drill a hole in his skull to relieve the pressure. Doctors couldn’t assure them their son would survive, they said. Twelve high school football players in the US have died from heat over the last decade, according to statistics compiled by the National Center for Catastrophic Sport Injury Research. Trumpler was released after two days in the hospital. Later, his parents said, they sent his medical records to Bowie High School and tried to discuss what had gone wrong. But they said the school’s athletic staff infuriated them by suggesting they hadn’t done enough to alert coaches about his condition during the game, Trumpler’s father told Reuters. A month later, Trumpler’s parents saw a video of an official for the governing body for Texas high school sports, the University Interscholastic League, referring to their son’s injury as a “questionable” heat-related incident. Neither the school district nor the UIL official responded to requests for comment. In an interview, UIL Executive Director Jamey Harrison said that the organization relies on schools to report the details of medical events and avoids instituting rules based on individual incidents. Heat storms are starting to reshape Texas football. State filings show that since the beginning of this year, at least four school districts in the state have registered to build indoor or covered practice spaces, two with price tags in excess of $10 million. And this year, the UIL adopted new rules requiring rest breaks, ice baths and shortenings or cancellations of practices in high heat. Yet these rules are not mandatory for football games themselves. Two weeks after his hospitalization, as Heat Storm Vera continued baking Austin, Trumpler resumed playing football. He declined to speak to Reuters, but wrote on X at the time that “it felt so good to return.” His heat injury, however, seemed to throw off college recruiters. Division I teams, those with the biggest and best programs, stopped calling, Trumpler’s father recalled. His mother said Trumpler himself seemed tepid about the prospect, which had once been his dream, and he is not currently attending college. “Our son, Justice, is tough and built for football, mentally and physically,” she wrote at the time. “This heat was tougher.” SPAIN, AUGUST 2023: “PIRATES OF LIQUID GOLD” Early in the morning of August 30, 2023, a team of thieves carefully maneuvered a tanker truck through the winding roads of the small Spanish town of Carcabuey, intent on an audacious heist. Around 2:30 a.m., according to a local police official, the thieves pulled into a gated driveway on the edge of town. They shut off lights and cut through the rickety gate’s padlock. They left no fingerprints because they wore gloves. Once inside, they beelined for their unusual loot: extra virgin olive oil, which they siphoned from industrial-sized tanks. Over the previous several months, a series of heat storms had helped fuel a drought that devastated the olive crop and sent the price of olive oil skyrocketing, raising the value of the stolen 56 metric tons to a staggering $546,000. Journalists nicknamed the thieves the Pirates of Liquid Gold. By dawn, when the olive mill’s manager, Martín Parras, arrived, all that remained was an oil streak on the driveway. Parras was so overcome, he said, that he walked into a nearby olive grove, sat beneath the trees and wept. In Spain’s southern region around Carcabuey, houses are painted white to repel the sun, and residents take long breaks during the hot afternoons. Olive trees, which evolved to have formidable heat tolerance, have thrived here for centuries. But the trees have struggled in the new heat storm era. Between March 12 and August 1, when Vera first reached Carcabuey, the little town endured eight other heat storms that rolled one into the next with almost no break. The combination of early heat and scarce rain burned the olive flowers, preventing them from opening and pollinating, Parras said. In the past five to 10 years, locals say, the heat that once lasted from June to August can now stretch from April to November, and it stays hot later into the evening. “People used to go out around 7 or 8 in summers but now it can be 9 or 9:30 and there’s no one in the streets,” said Juan Lara, who has been running a pastry shop near Carcabuey for 46 years. Heat Storm Vera spent a total of 127 days over Carcabuey. At first, Vera teased the city, brushing it briefly before smothering the town for three weeks until a couple of days before the theft. Temperatures surpassed 40 C (104 F) several times. Parras said about half the olives at his Marín Serrano El Lagar mill ended up unusable, with scant flesh and barely any oil. “Olive trees had a yellow color like when grass dries, and leaves fell,” he recalled. “It was monstrous.” The price of olive oil spiked by 44% that year, largely because the withering heat and drought reduced output by roughly half in Spain, the world’s largest producer. Some Spanish supermarkets placed alarms on bottles to prevent theft, but no one thought thieves would target a mill’s huge metal tanks. At Marín Serrano El Lagar, the only alarms were in the office and a room storing oil that was already bottled. Spanish police arrested a 50-year-old man who had crushed olives at the mill for more than two decades until he left in 2020 after an argument over his salary. Authorities suspect the man conspired to steal the oil with the owner of a rival mill just down the road, the local police official said. The owner was also arrested. Both men were later released, but remain under investigation. They told Reuters they did not steal the oil, with the 50-year-old suspect saying he’s eager to clear his name. The real culprit, according to mill manager Parras, has not been indicted. “Climate change has completely affected olive fields,” he said. “Has it been the cause of the theft? Totally.” If the heat hadn’t driven the price so high, he added, “There would have been no theft.” BRAZIL, SEPTEMBER 2023: DEATH OF THE DOLPHINS On September 28, 2023, an environmental scientist named Ayan Fleischmann sat in a small boat at the heart of a vast Amazonian lake and watched a dolphin die. The creature moved in jagged circles, its body shuddering. Suddenly, it sank. As Fleischmann watched the dolphin vanish into the darkness of Lake Tefé, smoke from nearby wildfires fouled the air. An algal bloom stained the waters blood-red. Dozens of dolphin corpses dotted the lake’s beaches. Photos taken by Fleischmann’s team show the dolphins’ skin wrinkled like melted plastic or peeling to reveal yellow flesh. This, Fleischmann recalled thinking, might be what Hell looks like. With its distinctive pink color, the river dolphin is one of the Amazon’s most iconic and mythologized creatures. According to legend, they would transform into humans at night to seduce locals. The dolphin was put on the endangered species list eight years ago, after poaching and rainforest destruction caused its numbers to plummet. Now, heat storms have emerged as an urgent new threat. Heat Storm Vera settled over the Amazon in late July and spent a total of nearly seven months over Lake Tefé, simmering it for 42 days in a row before Fleischmann watched the dolphin die. The heat storm helped warm the lake to a high of 41 C (105.8 F) – the temperature of a standard jacuzzi. For the dolphins, such temperatures were catastrophic: Fleischmann’s research team later concluded that the creatures had effectively been cooked alive. Fleischmann, 34, had been studying how the waters of Lake Tefé were changing for several years. “It became a friend. I see it every day,” he said. But as the heat storm festered, he recalled, so much of the lake dried up that when he and his colleagues visited local villages, they were pelted by whirlwinds of sand whipped up from newly exposed beaches. Later, Fleischmann’s research institute autopsied the dolphins that washed up on the lake’s shores. Temperatures were so high that most of the corpses rotted faster than they could be studied, said Hilda Chávez-Pérez, a biologist who oversaw the study of the bodies. But in those they could examine, she said, the researchers kept finding that the dolphins’ brains were bruised and their organs speckled with blood: telltale signs of heat stress. Many had empty stomachs, indicating that they had lost the ability to feed in the heat. The lake’s normal population is at least 700 river dolphins, said Fleischmann, but during September and October, when Vera scalded the area for all but one day, more than 200 died. “Nobody had ever seen that magnitude of mortality,” he said. “It was like a death circus.” POLAND, FEBRUARY 2024: WEIRD WINTERS In Poland’s Tatra Mountains, the first months of 2024 were full of strange signs. In mid-February, bears woke from hibernation weeks early and began roaming the ranges. Frogs also emerged early, ranger Tomasz Zając remembered, rising from the rotting leaves and underwater silt beneath which they had hunkered through the cold months. Although snow still clung to the high peaks, it was so slushy that it frequently slipped in mini-avalanches that left black scars of exposed rock.

While heat storms are hottest in summer, they can also mellow typically frigid months. Heat Storm Vera, which enveloped the Tatras for 31 days in January and February, sent the temperature up to 17 C (62.6 F). In neighboring Germany, Vera prompted the country’s weather service to tell people to leave behind their warm coats as they celebrated the annual winter carnival, while in the UK, television hosts joked about unusually “hot and steamy” Valentine’s Day temperatures in the English town of Lover. But winter heat storms can also cause unexpected harm. In January of this year, bone-chilling cold descended on eastern Canada and the US, causing Toronto to endure 23 straight days of sub-freezing cold and gripping parts of Minnesota in temperatures that plunged to minus 41.7 C (minus 43 F). Paradoxically, those frigid temperatures were largely caused by winter heat waves in the northern polar regions and Greenland, where residents basked in unseasonably balmy days that reached 11.3 C (52.3 F). That northern mass of warm air shunted a cold front down over eastern North America, in what climatologists call a polar vortex. Tennessee got so cold that freezing rain encased trees in ice, causing many to collapse under the weight. Forest silence was occasionally broken by a sound resembling gunshots as sap froze and expanded, splintering tree trunks. Almost half of Pittsburgh’s snowplows stopped working, forcing the city to leave roads uncleared for days and trash on the streets for a week. The extreme cold killed at least 100 people across the US, caused power losses for more than a million customers, drove more flight cancellations than any time since the COVID 19 pandemic, and forced school closures from Milwaukee to Atlanta. Even in Cuba, farmers woke to frost on their crops.

Heat Storm Vera spent weeks over Europe in January and February, effectively transforming winter into spring. By mid-February, local media estimated that a quarter of European ski resorts were closed due to lack of snow. It was so warm that many resorts couldn’t even [USN:L8N3EQ4AM TEXT:"make"] artificial powder. Amid the unseasonal heat, intense rain battered parts of Europe and neighboring countries; as Vera settled over the southern Turkish city of Antalya, flash floods inundated entire neighborhoods, with the sudden flow submerging fire trucks and buses. In the Tatra Mountains, winter’s end is marked by the blossoming of crocuses. More than a hundred million typically bloom starting in mid- to late-March, turning the valleys into purple oceans. Rangers have to patrol Chochołowska Glade – where crocuses bloom most densely – to prevent tourists stampeding the flowers into the ground. In late February, that frenzy was supposed to be weeks away. But on February 29, ranger Zając noticed a flash of color amidst Chochołowska’s freshly-uncovered grass. He squatted to get a better look at the purple petals unfolding around an orange stamen. Earlier than he could ever remember, the first crocus had arrived. THE PHILIPPINES, APRIL 2024: COLLAPSING CHILDREN Partway through April 2024, on the top floor of Saghakan High School in the Philippines’ Tacloban City, Jeffrey Polido was giving a lesson on typhoons to 50 sweating 14-year-olds in a concrete classroom with two rickety fans. Interrupting him, a student burst through the door with news: Yet another child had collapsed. Polido – a 37-year-old science teacher who at that time ran the school’s health clinic – raced outside to the stricken girl and took her vitals. He and the student who had alerted him carried the child down several flights of stairs to the clinic to recover. Then, Polido walked back to his roasting classroom and resumed teaching, knowing it would happen all over again. After all, he told Reuters, he had already seen dozens of students collapse. Polido, along with the teacher who comforted the student with the gushing nosebleed, didn’t know it but they were on the frontline of Heat Storm Vera. The heat was intensified by its most dangerous accomplice: humidity. As a result, a temperature of 33 C (91.4 F) in steamy Tacloban felt like 47 C (116.5 F), while hotter parts of the Philippines reached “feels like” levels of 53 C (127.5 F) – at which point the country’s weather bureau warned, “Heat stroke is imminent.” For the millions of children in schools cooled only by fans, the thick muggy heat was especially dangerous. In Manila, Jenita Simangan, 49, watched her 50-strong class of five-year-olds break out into rashes, complain of headaches, and say the heat made their skin feel like it was burning, she recalled. Partway through the heat spell, she said, one five-year-old staggered into class and began vomiting uncontrollably. As the child stood in a puddle of watery bile speckled with half-digested chunks of lunch, Simangan felt herself panic. It was the worst moment she’d experienced in two decades of teaching, she said. Heat Storm Vera hit Tacloban particularly hard, tormenting the city for a total of more than nine months. Standing in a rare spot of shade at Sagkahan High School earlier this year, Cloe Novella, 17, recalled sitting in her class and trying to catch the weak breeze from one of the classroom’s old fans when she realized one of her best friends hadn’t said anything since they sat down. Turning around, Novella saw her friend appeared to be sleeping, tapped her, and quickly realized that her friend had lost consciousness. Novella’s teacher told one of her classmates to fetch Polido, who came and carried the student to the clinic, where she recovered. She was one of more than 40 who Polido estimated fainted during Vera. The Philippines soon suspended in-person classes across the country and has since changed its school calendar to avoid exposing students to the most extreme temperatures. Yet for Novella and her fellow students, Heat Storm Vera kickstarted a new era of near-perpetual heat. LJ Corsanes, 17, said he frequently plunges into temperature-induced panic attacks. “It’s like going into a fight,” he said of going outside. “It’s like opening a door to hell.” Over the entire 1960s, heat storms hit Tacloban for only 7 days, and the city experienced 245 days of ordinary heat waves. This decade, ordinary heat waves have touched Tacloban for fewer than 40 days – but heat storms have engulfed the city for more than 1,470 days. That’s over 200 days a year. Tropical archipelagos such as the Philippines are particularly vulnerable to heat storms, Reuters’ analysis shows. The warm ocean heats the air from below while sunshine not only beats down from above but also reflects off the surrounding water. Other tropical islands, such as Guam, Haiti and much of Indonesia, spend most of the year in heat storms. The implacable heat is forcing students to learn grim new skills. In July, Polido gathered 80-odd teenagers for first aid training with the Red Cross. Over two days, they practiced how to begin chest compressions, how to lift an unconscious person to safety, and how to position someone who has passed out so they don’t choke on their tongues. For some, the heat has become eerily normal. Novella said it makes her feel “like I am burning in pain and fire.” But, she added, “It is not strange, because I am used to feeling the heat already.” IVORY COAST, NOVEMBER 2023-JUNE 2024: DEATH OF A CHOCOLATE CHIEF In his half-century as a farmer of cocoa, the raw ingredient of chocolate, Chief Brou Kouassi earned enough money to marry five times, send his 12 children to school, and float a little cash to his neighbors. He even had a nickname – “À Nous Deux”, or “Just Between Us” – a phrase people used when they came seeking assistance on the hush-hush. In 2023, Heat Storm Vera started stalking Digrikro, the village in western Ivory Coast where Kouassi had been chief since 2000. At first, the heat storm came and went, lurking for up to two weeks at a time. Then, beginning November 1, Vera besieged the area for more than four months straight, sometimes sending temperatures above 38 C (100.4 F). “La secheresse” – the drought – also began in November, according to local farmers and United Nations rainfall data. His sons had taken over the hard labor, but every morning Kouassi still pulled on his boots and went out to survey his 22-hectare farm. As Heat Storm Vera shriveled the pods and sent brittle leaves falling from the branches, Kouassi would shake his head and lament that he had never seen so many trees dead or dying. His sons would go out in the morning with their machetes to cut down the cocoa pods but return just a few hours later because, as Kouassi’s son Jules put it, “the trees didn’t give us anything.” Jules said the cocoa yield on his portion of the land for February to April 2024, an important harvesting time, was less than half of normal. Ivory Coast and its neighbor Ghana produce about 50% of the world’s cocoa. But in the wake of Heat Storm Vera, the harvest in those two countries fell by half. Vera had collaborators , among them disease, which preys more easily on heat-and-drought-weakened cocoa trees, and an El Niño, which likely intensified the heat storm. But Vera and the drought it exacerbated were relentless, with the heat storm lingering over one cocoa region of Ghana for a total of almost 11 months. In 2024, the price of cocoa [USN:L4N3NV05L TEXT:"almost tripled"]. In West Africa, where almost all the cocoa is produced by smallholder farms such as Kouassi’s, the stakes were existential. Kouassi urged his sons to abandon cocoa for heat-resistant crops such as rubber or cashews. “He kept saying, ‘If you don’t replace the cocoa trees, you’ll have nothing to eat,’” recalled Jules. In June 2024, as Heat Storm Vera took its last licks at Digrikro, Kouassi fell ill. After a medicinal broth of leaves didn’t work, his family sent him to the hospital, where Jules recalls doctors saying his father had malaria and anemia. He spent four days in the hospital, at a cost of 320,000 CFA, or about $525. But his illness persisted, so they sent him back again, paying another $525. They considered a third trip for the same high cost, but they couldn’t afford to keep sending him back because the devastation of the cocoa crop had beggared the family. Kouassi’s one-story concrete farmhouse offered little respite from the clammy heat. As his illness worsened – swelling that began in his feet spread all the way up to his thighs – he struggled to sleep more than a few hours each night. With money scarce and Western medicine failing, he asked to go to the village where he was born to visit a traditional healer or, if that failed, to be buried next to his parents. Kouassi traveled by bus, which typically takes more than six hours to cover the 200 kilometers, much of it on a choppy dirt road. Years earlier, before heat storms shattered his livelihood, Kouassi had built an eight-bedroom house there with a large patio, where he relished visits from relatives and neighbors, some whispering hush-hush stories. His sons hoped the more comfortable environment and traditional remedies might help him regain his health. The healer took 90,000 CFA, a little less than $160, then refused any more payments even though he kept bringing clay pots filled with medicinal concoctions. But his father continued to decline, Jules recalled, and finally pulled his son aside and asked him “to take care of the family because he didn’t know if he would survive.” Kouassi died on October 27, 2024, aged 68. No official cause of death was given. His beloved cocoa farm has not recovered. Many of the trees are dead or sick, Jules said, and revenue remains in a rut. Kouassi himself lies buried under a blank headstone, his family unable to afford the finishing tribute: a name plaque. Nor have they been able to raise enough money for a traditional funeral, a fact that torments Jules. In the culture of their Baoulé ethnic group, the failure to hold that ceremony – complete with a sheep sacrifice, drumming and dancing – means his father cannot go peacefully into the afterlife. “It’s like his soul is still walking around here,” Jules said, “unable to rest.” FEBRUARY, 2026: A MASSIVE NEW HEAT STORM Over its lifetime, Heat Storm Vera drifted over nearly 85% of the planet, more than any heat storm on record. Its peak size, covering 31.3% of the Earth on January 5, 2024, was also a record. Until this summer. Heat Storm Raimundo, which broiled Europe and stoked massive wildfires in Spain and France, extended over 33.8% of the globe on August 28. Since its inception on February 28, 2026, Raimundo has touched almost three quarters of the planet’s surface. Both heat storms spent time over a melting Nepalese glacier before its collapse on August 26 and the catastrophic flooding that followed, killing thousands. Early indications suggest that [USN:L1N45814P TEXT:"warming temperatures contributed"] to the collapse of the glacier and the bedrock beneath it. Up until the glacier gave way, it had spent about 58% of this decade in a heat storm or heat wave, up from 7% during the 1960s. For the six days immediately preceding its collapse, the glacier had been blanketed by Heat Storm Raimundo. Raimundo isn’t yet finished. It has been heating the earth for 235 days and counting.

item.title: Kremlin hopes Witkoff can brief Putin soon on latest Ukrainian/European thinking on peace deal
item.description: The Kremlin said on Tuesday that it hoped a meeting in Russia between President Vladimir Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff could be organised in the near future to discuss the Ukraine peace process and a range of "very important issues."
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Kremlin said on Tuesday that it hoped a meeting in Russia between President Vladimir Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff could be organised in the near future to discuss the Ukraine peace process and a range of "very important issues." Witkoff is [USN:L1N466099 TEXT:"expected to hold talks"] in Oslo on Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and representatives from the E4 – made up of Britain, France, Germany, and Poland. Officials from the European Union and NATO are also expected to attend. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Witkoff could brief Putin on the position of the Ukrainians and Europeans when they met. "We hope that a meeting can be arranged in the very near future, and that the American negotiators, Mr Witkoff, will be able to brief President Putin on their contacts with both the Ukrainians and the Europeans, as well as to continue the exchange of views between Washington and Moscow on a whole range of very important issues. We consider such meetings to be of great importance on every occasion; they are always timely and very substantive, and we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators," Peskov told reporters. He did not give further details. Some US media have reported that Witkoff may meet Putin on Wednesday in St Petersburg. A recent call between Putin and Trump produced an agreement on [USN:L8N4610WB TEXT:"Russian diesel supplies"], which Trump said could lower prices but which alarmed Ukraine and European allies.

item.title: ByteDance, Alibaba e Tencent fazem pedidos de chips da Nvidia no valor de mais de US$35 bi
item.description: As empresas ByteDance, Alibaba e Tencent encomendaram mais de 3 milhões das novas placas de vídeo RTX PRO 5500 da Nvidia, com um valor de tabela total superior a US$35 bilhões, segundo duas fontes a par do assunto, em uma corrida para obter um chip menos potente, mas que cumpra as normas de exportação, em meio às restrições dos EUA ao comércio com a China.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: As empresas ByteDance, Alibaba e Tencent encomendaram mais de 3 milhões das novas placas de vídeo RTX PRO 5500 da Nvidia, com um valor de tabela total superior a US$35 bilhões, segundo duas fontes a par do assunto, em uma corrida para obter um chip menos potente, mas que cumpra as normas de exportação, em meio às restrições dos EUA ao comércio com a China. A fabricante de chips norte-americana Nvidia (NVDA.O) informou a clientes e parceiros que não pode garantir o atendimento dos pedidos, pois a demanda das empresas de tecnologia chinesas excede em muito a produção planejada, segundo as duas fontes e uma terceira pessoa a par do assunto. Elas pediram anonimato por não estarem autorizadas a falar com a mídia. O RTX PRO 5500 é um chip para estações de trabalho, projetado para computadores profissionais potentes, e não para os grandes clusters de data centers que utilizam os processadores de IA mais avançados da Nvidia. No entanto, ele está entre os chips mais potentes da Nvidia que ainda estão disponíveis para compradores chineses. O chip para data center B300 da Nvidia, baseado na arquitetura Blackwell, não pode ser vendido a compradores chineses devido aos controles de exportação dos EUA, enquanto as exportações do H200, baseado na arquitetura Hopper, são analisadas caso a caso e estão sujeitas a condições de licenciamento. Uma fonte afirmou que a Nvidia informou aos parceiros que eles poderiam receber apenas 5% a 10% das quantidades solicitadas. Outra fonte disse que a empresa havia indicado que não poderia produzir mais do que 3 milhões de placas RTX PRO 5500 globalmente em 2027. O total de pedidos de clientes na China ultrapassou 6 milhões, segundo duas das fontes. Os pedidos das três gigantes chinesas de tecnologia são por placas com preço de cerca de US$11.400 cada, disseram duas das fontes, o que lhes confere um valor potencial combinado de mais de US$35 bilhões. A magnitude dos pedidos, que não havia sido divulgada anteriormente, ressalta o interesse contínuo das empresas chinesas pelo hardware da Nvidia, apesar das restrições dos EUA. O presidente-executivo da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, afirmou que as restrições reduziram a participação da Nvidia no mercado chinês de chips para data centers de IA de um quase monopólio a praticamente nada. Mas a demanda pelo RTX PRO 5500 sugere que a Nvidia mantém um mercado potencial considerável na China por meio de produtos menos potentes que ainda podem estar disponíveis. O aumento na demanda também destaca como as restrições dos EUA restringiram o fornecimento de poder de computação na segunda maior economia do mundo, à medida que as empresas chinesas correm para desenvolver modelos de IA de ponta e impulsionam os esforços de Pequim para implantar a tecnologia em todos os seus setores. As restrições de Washington levaram as empresas chinesas a recorrerem a fornecedores nacionais, enquanto Pequim tem incentivado o uso de chips de fabricação própria. A Huawei, em particular, ganhou participação de mercado, embora os fabricantes chineses de chips tenham, em geral, enfrentado dificuldades para se equiparar aos principais produtos norte-americanos, em parte porque restrições específicas limitaram o acesso aos equipamentos estrangeiros utilizados na fabricação dos chips mais avançados. Um porta-voz da Nvidia afirmou que os fabricantes chineses de chips e placas para estações de trabalho tiveram “um crescimento sem precedentes desde 2022”, quando as restrições foram impostas pela primeira vez. A ByteDance, Alibaba (9988.HK) e a Tencent (0700.HK) não responderam aos pedidos de comentário. O Departamento de Indústria e Segurança do Departamento de Comércio dos EUA, que supervisiona os controles de exportação, e o Ministério da Indústria e Tecnologia da Informação da China não responderam aos pedidos de comentário. (Reportagem da equipe da Reuters)

item.title: Meet the heat storm: 7 takeaways from our investigation that gave supersized heat waves a new name
item.description: Heat waves have evolved from sporadic, isolated episodes to massive, cascading weather events that can blanket vast swaths of the planet for months or even years at a time.
item.dc:creator: Maurice Tamman
item.content:encoded: Heat waves have evolved from sporadic, isolated episodes to massive, cascading weather events that can blanket vast swaths of the planet for months or even years at a time. To continue calling such sprawling phenomena “heat waves” would be like calling a monsoon a rain shower. To understand the new reality of these immense expanses of heat, Reuters consulted with two dozen climate researchers and analyzed temperatures around the globe for every hour of every day since 1960. From those results, we developed a new concept: the “heat storm.” Scientists and researchers often discuss global warming in the context of risks that will arise if the planet’s average global temperature rises more than 2°C (3.6°F) above pre-industrial levels. What is an ordinary person to make of that? Not much. Heat waves are the connective tissue between the science of global warming and our everyday experience. But supersized heat waves used to be rare. No longer. Now they swarm the planet. Naming events is “a powerful way for people to understand that something is happening,” Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, told Reuters. Yet “we don't do that with heat waves,” he said, even though heat has been estimated to kill almost half a million people a year. These are the key findings of the Reuters investigation, The Age of Heat Storms : WHAT IS A HEAT STORM? There is no universal definition of a heat wave. So, in consultation with climate scientists, we have defined an ordinary heat wave as five or more consecutive days of abnormally high temperatures. We call the largest heat waves – those that at their peak cover at least 1% of the globe, roughly half the size of Canada – heat storms . MORE AND BIGGER Heat storms were rare in the 1960s, when they averaged about five active storms per year. This decade, heat storms have averaged about 102 a year. One of them caused this summer’s deadly heat in Europe. BIOGRAPHY OF A 367-DAY HEAT STORM The largest heat storm on record, named Heat Storm Vera, lasted for 367 days over 2023-2024 and swept over nearly 85% of the globe. Reuters tells the story of how Vera impacted every corner of the world, from a football player going to the hospital in Texas, to Amazonian river dolphins dying in a “circus of death,” to a cocoa farmer whose livelihood was destroyed in Ivory Coast. GREENHOUSE GAS EMISSIONS As greenhouse gas emissions have increased, so too have heat storms and ordinary heat waves. From the 1960s to this decade, the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has increased by more than 30%. Over that time, the average portion of the planet likely to be covered by heat storms and heat waves has risen more than 12-fold. 18 YEARS WITHOUT A BREAK Another new phenomenon we identified: heat storms that run consecutively, simultaneously, or both — heat storm cascades. The duration of these cascades swelled from an average of roughly two months in the 1960s to nine months in the early 2000s. Then, on July 6, 2008, a cascade started — and still has not stopped. For more than 18 years straight, at least one heat storm has been roiling the planet, and often more than one. WE ARE IN A HEAT STORM NOW The world is now in the grip of Heat Storm Raimundo, which broiled Europe and stoked massive wildfires in Spain and France this summer. Since its inception on February 28, 2026, Raimundo has touched almost three-quarters of the planet’s surface. LIVE TOOL TO TRACK HEAT STORMS As part of this series, Reuters has created an online Heat Storm Tracker that names and follows heat storms in real time. This is now a feature of the Reuters Climate Monitor, which offers ways to understand major weather events and measure how the planet is warming.

item.title: El calendario de liberación de reservas de petróleo de la AIE depende de cada país, dice su director
item.description: El calendario para la liberación de 20 millones de barriles de diésel procedentes de las reservas de emergencia de los miembros de la Agencia Internacional de la Energía depende de cada país y de la situación del mercado petrolero, declaró el martes el máximo responsable de la agencia.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: El calendario para la liberación de 20 millones de barriles de diésel procedentes de las reservas de emergencia de los miembros de la Agencia Internacional de la Energía depende de cada país y de la situación del mercado petrolero, declaró el martes el máximo responsable de la agencia. La AIE decidió la semana pasada acelerar la liberación del petróleo restante de una liberación récord de reservas de emergencia prometida en marzo, incluidos más de 20 millones de barriles de diésel, lo antes posible para impulsar el suministro y frenar la escalada de los precios. "La cantidad que se libere y el momento en que se haga dependerá de los países y de la situación de los mercados en invierno", dijo el director ejecutivo de la AIE, Fatih Birol, en una conferencia celebrada en Londres y organizada por el Financial Times. La AIE coordina las liberaciones de petróleo de las reservas de emergencia por parte de los países industrializados. En marzo, los países se comprometieron a liberar más de 400 millones de barriles de crudo y productos petrolíferos ante la escalada de los precios.

item.title: Meta's AI spending, Muse assistant adoption in focus for quarterly results
item.description: Meta's massive artificial intelligence outlays and adoption of its Muse personal assistant will be in focus when it reports third-quarter results on Wednesday, as the social media firm seeks to show that its AI investments can sustain growth.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Meta's massive artificial intelligence outlays and adoption of its Muse personal assistant will be in focus when it reports third-quarter results on Wednesday, as the social media firm seeks to show that its AI investments can sustain growth. The company (META.O) has rolled out several [USN:L4N45K0VY TEXT:"AI products and services"] targeting businesses as CEO Mark Zuckerberg looks to create a new revenue stream beyond advertising to compete better in the AI race with OpenAI and Anthropic. Positive reception for Meta's [USN:L6N4500XV TEXT:"Muse assistant"], which offers subscriptions, and its [USN:L4N45Y13Q TEXT:"latest AI models"] have boosted investor confidence in the company's AI strategy, as Meta commits hundreds of billions of dollars to expanding its AI infrastructure "Recent AI launches have strengthened confidence in the company's AI execution," BofA Global Research analysts said, adding that its survey also suggests healthy ad demand in the quarter Analysts estimate Meta's capital expenditure more than doubled to $41.68 billion in the September quarter, according to Visible Alpha data The rising spending had squeezed its free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect it to report a cash burn of $8.52 billion in the third quarter Morgan Stanley analysts raised their earnings estimates for 2027 and 2028 for Meta despite higher spending, citing stronger ad growth and the potential for new AI products to generate additional revenue Wall Street expects Meta to report a decline of about 17% in net income to $15.44 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG Meta is set to report revenue growth of 23.8% to $63.42 billion, slowing from about 28% in the previous quarter amid intense competition from Google and TikTok Shares of the company have gained about 7% this year, underperforming a roughly 12% rise in the benchmark S&P 500

item.title: Sharks seek first regulation win of season as they face Canadiens
item.description: Macklin Celebrini and the San Jose Sharks face Nick Suzuki and the host Montreal Canadiens in an East-meets-West showdown on Tuesday night.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Macklin Celebrini and the San Jose Sharks face Nick Suzuki and the host Montreal Canadiens in an East-meets-West showdown on Tuesday night. Tuesday's tilt is the first of two meetings between the teams this season. The Sharks swept the series last season and have won two of their last three in Montreal. San Jose is 1-1-1 on its current six-game road trip and still seeking its first regulation win of the season. It's also playing on the tail end of a back-to-back, falling 3-1 to the Maple Leafs in Toronto on Monday evening. In that game, Mason Marchment gave the Sharks a 1-0 lead in the first period, but penalty trouble ultimately ended up in the back of the visitors' net. Auston Matthews and Gavin McKenna scored power-play goals, while Nick Paul scored into an empty net late in the final frame. Yaroslav Askarov made 29 saves for San Jose in the loss. "Whatever you want to call it, 'puck luck' or just bounces, but at the end of the day, I've had a lot of chances and guys in our room have gotten a lot of chances that they're kicking themselves about," Celebrini said. "We're not playing bad hockey. We're losing one-goal games. ... We're in all of these games. It's just the little stuff. The details that cost us games down the stretch. And tonight, not executing when we needed to." The Sharks have allowed third-period goals in each of their games on the current road trip. "There's definitely room for improvement when you give up a goal like that two games in a row," Sharks head coach Ryan Warsofsky said following a 4-3 shootout loss to the Detroit Red Wings over the weekend. "A lot of it is just getting the details right and understanding where we are in the game." Meanwhile, the Canadiens are looking for their first regulation win since their season opener on Sept. 29. Montreal has won three of its last four games: 1-0 against the Red Wings in the shootout, 4-3 versus Buffalo in the shootout, and another 4-3 win against the Sabres in overtime. In the overtime victory, the Habs took a 3-2 lead into the third period, but Tage Thompson tied the game at 10:12. Cole Caufield, who also scored Montreal's second goal of the night, netted the game-winning goal 54 seconds into overtime when he finished a breakaway by scoring on the blocker side on Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen. Juraj Slafkovsky and Alexandre Carrier each had two assists in the victory, and Jacob Fowler made 23 saves. "Buffalo is not an easy team to play when you have a lead," Canadiens head coach Martin St. Louis said. "They open up their game a lot, and you have to be calculated with your decisions. Even in the offensive zone, you can't make 'almost' plays. The 'almosts' are the plays that they live for. They're hoping you make an 'almost,' and then it goes the other way." --Field Level Media
