item.title: IEA oil stocks release timing is up to individual members, chief says
item.description: The timeline for the release of 20 million barrels of diesel from International Energy Agency members' emergency reserves depends on individual countries and the oil market situation, the agency's top official said on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The timeline for the release of 20 million barrels of diesel from International Energy Agency members' emergency reserves depends on individual countries and the oil market situation, the agency's top official said on Tuesday. The IEA [USN:L1N4610MY TEXT:"decided last week"] to accelerate the release of oil remaining from a record emergency reserves release pledged in March, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible to boost supply and cool soaring prices. "How much is released and when depends on the countries, depends on the situation of winter markets," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said at a conference in London organised by the Financial Times. The IEA coordinates industrialised nations' releases of oil from emergency stocks. In March, countries had pledged to release more than 400 million barrels of crude and oil products as prices soared.

item.title: Seúl promete un "castigo contundente" tras las amenazas de Pionyang de reforzar la frontera
item.description: Corea del Sur prometió este martes una respuesta severa si Corea del Norte lleva a cabo sus amenazas de reforzar su presencia militar a lo largo de la frontera, lo que ha avivado las tensiones en la península de Corea.
item.dc:creator: Kyu-Seok Shim
item.content:encoded: Corea del Sur prometió este martes una respuesta severa si Corea del Norte lleva a cabo sus amenazas de reforzar su presencia militar a lo largo de la frontera, lo que ha avivado las tensiones en la península de Corea. En un comunicado, el Ministerio de Defensa de Seúl expresó su profunda preocupación por las amenazas de Pionyang de desplegar más armas de ataque táctico a lo largo de la frontera y reanudar las emisiones por altavoces hacia el Sur. La escalada y el intercambio de amenazas han aumentado la posibilidad de enfrentamientos en la frontera, fuertemente armada, y socavan los avances diplomáticos logrados por el presidente surcoreano, Lee Jae-myung, poco después de asumir el cargo. El ministerio afirmó que las emisiones y los disparos de advertencia de Corea del Sur cerca de la Línea de Demarcación Militar (MDL, por sus siglas en inglés) constituían una "medida defensiva legítima" destinada a impedir incursiones y a obligar a los soldados norcoreanos que cruzaran la línea a retirarse. "Si Corea del Norte utiliza nuestras medidas legítimas como pretexto para llevar a cabo nuevas provocaciones, la castigaremos con contundencia", dijo el ministerio. Instó a Pionyang a que dejara de formular lo que calificó de afirmaciones infundadas, pusiera fin a las incursiones a través de la MDL y respondiera a los esfuerzos por resolver las diferencias entre ambas partes en torno a la línea. "CLARA PROVOCACIÓN" El presidente del Estado Mayor Conjunto de Seúl, Jin Young-seung, revisó la preparación militar durante una visita a un mando del ejército en primera línea y ordenó operaciones destinadas a reforzar la iniciativa de Seúl en la Zona Desmilitarizada, informó su ejército en un comunicado aparte. "No podemos tolerar que Corea del Norte califique falsamente nuestras medidas operativas legítimas como provocaciones y achaque la responsabilidad del aumento de las tensiones militares a nuestras Fuerzas Armadas", dijo Jin. Afirmó que Corea del Norte era responsable de colocar minas terrestres al sur de la MDL, que hirieron gravemente a soldados surcoreanos el mes pasado, y calificó el incidente de "clara provocación" y violación del acuerdo de armisticio. Las advertencias de Seúl se produjeron después de que Kim Yo-jong, hermana del líder norcoreano Kim Jong-un, acusara al ejército surcoreano de poner en peligro a los soldados norcoreanos al realizar disparos de advertencia mientras Pionyang llevaba a cabo trabajos de fortificación de la frontera. La amenaza de Kim Yo-jong de reanudar las emisiones norcoreanas por altavoces corre el riesgo de dar al traste con una medida clave de distensión que el presidente surcoreano, Lee Jae-myung, ha presentado como uno de los primeros logros de sus esfuerzos por reanudar la diplomacia con Pionyang. Corea del Norte lleva instalando minas y barreras a lo largo de la frontera desde abril de 2024. Corea del Sur dijo este mes que Pionyang había desplegado hasta 7.000 trabajadores en la zona este año y que personal norcoreano había cruzado la MDL en unas 50 ocasiones. Corea del Sur también ha detectado algunos cambios en las actividades militares de Corea del Norte cerca de las islas fronterizas situadas frente a su costa occidental, entre las dos Coreas, declaró el martes Ju Il-suk, comandante del Cuerpo de Marines de Corea del Sur, en una audiencia parlamentaria, sin dar más detalles. Añadió que Seúl estaba reforzando sus capacidades de vigilancia e inteligencia como respuesta. Los analistas señalaron que este enfrentamiento aumentaba el riesgo de un choque militar. "Si el umbral de Corea del Norte cae por debajo de las normas de intervención vigentes en Corea del Sur, la mera repetición de los procedimientos actuales podría bastar para crear las condiciones para un enfrentamiento", dijo Hong Min, investigador del Instituto Coreano para la Unificación Nacional. Michael Bosack, director fundador del Parley Policy Institute y antiguo responsable del Mando de las Naciones Unidas, señaló que los soldados podrían confundir los disparos de advertencia con ataques fallidos, lo que supondría el riesgo de "una interpretación errónea de las intenciones y posibles disparos de respuesta".

item.title: German ZEW investor morale falls more than expected as energy prices weigh
item.description: German investor morale fell more than expected in October, the ZEW economic institute said on Tuesday, ending a five-month run of improvements, as high energy prices weigh on private consumption and investment.
item.dc:creator: Linda Pasquini
item.content:encoded: German investor morale fell more than expected in October, the ZEW economic institute said on Tuesday, ending a five-month run of improvements, as high energy prices weigh on private consumption and investment. The index fell to 28.1 points. Analysts polled by Reuters had expected the reading to slip to 30 from 34.7 points [USN:APNACYQPF TEXT:"a month earlier"]. "Private consumption and investment remain weak because of high energy prices: they put real incomes under pressure, increase production costs and keep inflation higher for longer," said ZEW President Achim Wambach. German producer prices rose at their [USN:L8N4660AF TEXT:"fastest pace in three and a half years"] in September, the federal statistics office said earlier on Tuesday, driven by higher energy prices due to the Iran war. Higher oil and natural gas prices as a result of the conflict have slowed a long-awaited recovery in Europe's largest economy, which Wambach said was not self-sustaining despite slowly emerging from stagnation. Germany's governing coalition faces growing pressure from the rise of the far-right AfD, whose successes in recent state elections have intensified concerns among mainstream parties and exposed tensions within the governing alliance. The [USN:L1N45Y03X TEXT:"resignation of Labour Minister"] Baerbel Bas last week added to uncertainty. "The latest political developments are likely to have increased uncertainty regarding the swift implementation of the [USN:L8N45U0DJ TEXT:"reform"] plans announced in the summer," said Felicitas Henze, economist at Deutsche Bank Research. However, a reading by ZEW on views of the current economic situation improved more than expected to minus 35.9 points from minus 47.1 in September. The German economy ministry said [USN:L8N45U0IF TEXT:"earlier this month"] the Iran war was not hurting the economy as much as feared, as it raised its economic growth forecasts for this year and next. "Given the high level of outstanding orders, the industry will initially be able to increase its output. This is also the reason for the improved economic outlook," said Thomas Gitzel, chief economist at VP Bank. The German economy grew by 0.3% in the second quarter. A "surprisingly robust" first half should support growth in 2026, Gitzel said, with the ZEW survey indicating no significant new momentum in the last three months of the year after the economy likely made little progress in the third quarter. The results were based on ZEW survey responses from 178 analysts and institutional investors from October 12 to 19.

item.title: Google Cloud services face outage in London, Revolut services down too
item.description: Multiple Google Cloud services experienced disruptions in the company's London region on Tuesday, according to its service status page, while British digital bank Revolut also reported a service outage.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Multiple Google Cloud services experienced disruptions in the company's London region on Tuesday, according to its service status page, while British digital bank Revolut also reported a service outage. A person familiar with the matter told Reuters that Revolut's service outage was related to the Google Cloud service disruption. Revolut's status page showed most of its services were unavailable or partially unavailable, including card payments and ATM withdrawals. "We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers' money and data are safe," Revolut said on X. Google said its engineering team was investigating the issue, which impacted the London-based europe-west2 data center. Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google did not immediately respond to a Reuters request seeking further details. Separately, ING (INGA.AS) Germany said there were problems logging into online banking and its banking app due to a technical issue.

item.title: Boaz Weinstein’s UK feud tests watchdog's bite
item.description: The hedge fund manager is on the cusp of a board coup at a £1 bln Baillie Gifford investment company. His intention is unclear, but if he wants to appoint himself manager, forthcoming new UK rules should make that harder. The snag is that regulators' proposals may come too late.
item.dc:creator: Neil Unmack
item.content:encoded: Boaz Weinstein’s latest tilt at a UK trust may be a race against time. The hedge fund manager is looking to oust the board of a £1 billion ($1.3 billion) Baillie Gifford-managed investment company. What he plans to do afterwards isn’t totally clear. But it would all be a lot simpler if forthcoming UK rules on manager conflicts were already in place. Weinstein’s London [USN:L6N4060Q6 TEXT:"campaigns"] are a souped-up version of traditional fund activism. The ex-Deutsche Bank (DBKGn.DE) trader’s Saba Capital has sought to shake up boards at several investment trusts. Usually that means buying shares in unloved vehicles when they trade at a discount to net asset value, and then agitating for buybacks to close the gap. There’s no doubt that his campaigns have kept some otherwise sleepy directors on their toes - as has his financial muscle, which sees Saba frequently emerge as the biggest shareholder in its target trusts. Yet the board at his latest quarry, the Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust (USAB.L) , worries that Weinstein has a different agenda. Saba now holds around 30% of the company, and has twice unsuccessfully tried to oust the board. The fact that other shareholders mostly rejected his moves suggests they are happy with Baillie Gifford’s performance as manager. Indeed, the trust has beaten the S&P 500 Index (.SPX) since inception, thanks to bets on private companies like Anthropic. In short, it's exactly the kind of growth-focused investment vehicle that successive British governments have sought to promote. Weinstein's Saba has demanded that the board liquidate assets and hand back money to shareholders who want it - either at net asset value or very close to it. The board counters that the hedgie has already been offered that deal, and that he turned it down. It therefore worries that Weinstein wants to take control of the company for his own benefit, perhaps to get Saba appointed as manager. The Association of Investment Companies, a trade body for UK trusts, says this is a likely explanation. Saba declined to comment. If that is indeed Weinstein’s plan, he has a pretty good chance of making it happen. Saba and another US fund, a potential ally, hold nearly 38% of the trust’s shares. Assuming they join forces at a key vote this coming Friday, it would take a high turnout of close to 80% and full opposition from other shareholders to block the duo. And UK listing rules don’t stop asset managers with holdings in trusts from appointing themselves as manager. The Financial Conduct Authority is looking to close that loophole with a new set of reforms . They could mean, for example, that shares held by a manager are excluded from the vote on a trust’s investment strategy. Yet it's not clear when the rules will kick in: the FCA may not announce them until year-end. If the trust prevails against Weinstein in Friday's vote, the new rules may mean that there's less need in future to fret about Saba's intentions. Conversely, if Weinstein were able to take over management of the trust just ahead of a rule change, it would be an awkward outcome for regulators. ($1 = 0.7509 pounds) Follow @Unmack1 on X Shareholders in Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust will on October 23 vote at an annual general meeting on resolutions put forward by top shareholder Saba Capital. Saba is seeking to appoint three members to the currently five-strong board, including one of its own employees, James Waterlow. It has said it will support a “long overdue liquidity event”. The board of Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust says it has offered Saba a tender exit at close to net asset value, which has been rejected, and that it believes Saba is seeking to take control of the company for its own interests. The UK Financial Conduct Authority is consulting on changes to its listing rules for investment trusts. The changes seek to address conflicts of interest by, for example, preventing substantial shareholders who are also managers of trusts from voting on changes to investment policy. The reforms are set to be announced by the end of 2026. “Our proposals are designed to make sure there are appropriate safeguards against conflicts as markets evolve while preserving the important role of shareholder engagement and activism", an FCA spokesperson told Breakingviews. item.title: Ryanair CEO tells Europe to ready for biggest airfare hike in history
item.description: European airfares will see their "biggest increase in history" next year, Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary said on Tuesday, with airlines largely unhedged against higher jet fuel costs.
item.dc:creator: Philip Blenkinsop
item.content:encoded: European airfares will see their "biggest increase in history" next year, Ryanair (RYA.I) CEO Michael O'Leary said on Tuesday, with airlines largely unhedged against higher jet fuel costs. O'Leary forecast there would be fewer seats available next year as a result of bankruptcies and takeovers among airlines, which together with the unhedged positions would result in fares increasing by as much as 20%. "You're going to see airfares rise next year in Europe, I think by 10, 15, maybe 20%. You're going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 months," O'Leary told a news conference in Brussels. The Iran war has driven jet fuel prices sharply higher, squeezing margins for airlines that were unhedged. O'Leary said that Ryanair and other European airlines had strong hedge positions on jet fuel for 2026, adding that Europe's largest airline was 80% hedged at $67 per barrel to March 2027 when the conflict began at the end of February. The Ryanair CEO said that from April 2027 most European airlines had very little hedging in place. Ryanair has just 15% of its fuel costs for next year at $85 a barrel, compared with spot rates around double that level, he said. BOEING 737 MAX 10 CERTIFICATION O'Leary was in Brussels to announce he was cutting 20 routes and more than a million seats from Belgium for the airline's winter schedule after Belgian plans to increase its aviation tax to €7 in January from €2 now. The industry veteran also said he was optimistic that US certification of the Boeing (BA.N) 737 MAX 10 will be completed this month, allowing Ryanair to receive 16 planes in early 2027. "Boeing are hoping to have the MAX 10, the new aircraft, certified before the end of October ... We're pretty optimistic that that date will be hit," O'Leary told Reuters. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is expected to announce the Federal Aviation Administration [USN:L1N4650ZF TEXT:"has approved"] the long-delayed [USN:L1N45K0OS TEXT:"737 MAX 10"] on Tuesday after a glitch with its navigation software threatened further delay to certification.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz und Wirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche sehen Investitionszusagen von Hunderten Milliarden Euro in die deutsche Wirtschaft. Der Kanzler sprach am Dienstag bei der Konferenz "Invest in Germany" in Berlin von Zusagen der Unternehmen der Initiative "Made for Germany" in Höhe von 800 Milliarden Euro bis 2028. "Wir sehen ein beschleunigtes Wachstum im Jahr 2026 trotz steigenden geopolitischen Drucks und eines Sprungs der Energiepreise", fügte er hinzu. Das Wirtschaftsministerium sprach davon, dass in diesem Jahr 228,6 Milliarden Euro in Deutschland investiert würden - davon 95 Milliarden Euro aus dem Ausland. Der Kanzler verwies darauf, dass der Internationale Währungsfonds die Wachstumsannahme für Deutschland auf 1,3 Prozent in diesem Jahr erhöht habe. Die ausländischen Direktinvestitionen seien 2025 gegenüber 2024 um 50 Prozent auf 86 Milliarden Euro gestiegen. Er verwies zudem auf eine sprunghafte Zunahme neuer Start-ups. Ziel der Konferenz ist es, im globalen, aber auch innereuropäischen Wettbewerb Firmen zu Investitionen in den Standort Deutschland zu bewegen. Auch Frankreichs Präsident Emmanuel Macron hat bereits Investitionskonferenzen abgehalten. Allerdings werden auf solchen Konferenzen auch oft Summen von Investitionen zusammengezählt, die bereits vorher entschieden worden waren. So sprach etwa Sanofi-Chefin Belén Garijo davon, dass der Pharmakonzern bis 2032 zwei Milliarden Euro in Deutschland in die Insulin-Produktion stecke. Merz sowie etliche Ministerinnen und Minister der schwarz-roten Regierung warben gerade gegenüber ausländischen CEOs mit den Vorzügen Deutschlands. Die Bundesregierung versuche, diese Entwicklung mit entschiedenen Reformen der Sozialsysteme und dem Abbau von Bürokratie auf nationaler und europäischer Ebene zu unterstützen, sagte Merz. "Wichtig sind Tempo und Umsetzung", fügte er, ebenso wie Digitalminister Karsten Wildberger (CDU) in seinem Statement, hinzu. Als Stärken Deutschlands nannte der Kanzler die politische Stabilität, die gute Bonität, die Unabhängigkeit des Justizsystems, die multilaterale, verlässliche Ausrichtung des Landes, die starke Forschungslandschaft, die geografische Lage in der Mitte des EU-Binnenmarktes sowie die nach wie vor starke industrielle Basis. Er forderte die Firmen ebenso wie Reiche auf, verstärkt Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) bei ihrer Arbeit einzusetzen. MINISTER WERBEN IM SCHNELLDURCHLAUF In einer für Investitionskonferenzen üblichen sogenannten Schnellrunde warben Reiche, Wildberger, Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil (SPD), Bauministerin Verena Hubertz (SPD), Verkehrsminister Steffen Bilger (CDU), Forschungs- und Weltrauministerin Dorothee Bär (CSU) sowie der Investitionsbeauftragte des Kanzlers, Martin Blessing, für Investitionen in den von ihnen verantworteten Bereichen. "Ich will Ihr Geld", scherzte Vizekanzler Klingbeil und verwies darauf, dass die Regierung den Kapitalmarkt in Deutschland und Europa deutlich stärke. Ein Beispiel sei das neue geplante Kapitalmarkt-Element in der gesetzlichen Rentenversicherung nach schwedischem Vorbild. Es sollten insgesamt mehr Gelder am Kapitalmarkt angelegt werden, anstatt sie auf Sparkonten zu horten, sagte der SPD-Vorsitzende. Bauministerin Hubertz betonte, dass die Nachfrage nach Wohnungen enorm sei, weswegen sich Investitionen lohnten. Die SPD-Politikerin bekräftigte, Enteignungen großer Immobilienkonzerne, wie sie in Berlin auf Landesebene von der wahrscheinlich neuen Regierung geplant sind, durch ein Bundesgesetz zu unterbinden. Hubertz hatte zuvor bereits dem "Spiegel" gesagt, dass die Bundesregierung im staatlichen Deutschlandfonds über eine KfW-Investition von 100 Millionen Euro privates Kapital von einer Milliarde Euro für den Wohnungsbau mobilisieren wolle. Verkehrsminister Bilger (CDU) verwies auf die 500 Milliarden Euro für Infrastruktur in den kommenden Jahren, die für die Erneuerung eingesetzt würden. Es sei ein langfristig ausgerichteter Plan, der auch Möglichkeiten für Kooperationen mit privaten Investoren schaffe. Digitalminister Wildberger verwies auf die forcierte Digitalisierung der öffentlichen Verwaltung und den Abbau der Bürokratielasten für Unternehmen um 30 Prozent. Eine Studie der Beratungsgesellschaft Boston Consulting Group (BCG) hatte Deutschland zuvor großes Potenzial bei der KI-Entwicklung bescheinigt. Allerdings hätten Japan und Südkorea aufgeholt und seien in die Weltspitze vorgerückt. Deutschland trete dagegen auf der Stelle und sei nicht in der Weltspitze. Es fehlten vor allem Fachkräfte in dem Bereich.

item.title: Gulf Keystone, ShaMaran agree $601 million oil merger

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Gulf Keystone Petroleum (GKP.L) said on Tuesday it would merge with Norway's ShaMaran Petroleum (SNMS.OL) in a $601 million all-share 50-50 deal, creating one of the largest producers in Iraq's oil-rich Kurdistan region. Here are some details from the statement: ShaMaran shareholders to receive 0.07533958 Gulf Keystone share for each ShaMaran share held, with Gulf Keystone shareholders to receive a $50 million special dividend Merger combines operations across four Iraqi fields: Shaikan, Atrush, Sarsang and Hamrin Combined company expected to hold 323 million barrels of proved and probable reserves With pro-forma working interest production of 53,000 bpd, combined company ranks among the top 10 European listed independent oil producers Combined group has potential to reach 100,000 barrels of oil per day through development of Shaikan and Hamrin fields, a Gulf Keystone spokesperson said Dealmaking among Middle East-focused oil companies is supported by higher oil prices, with Genel Energy (GENL.L) competing with Norway's DNO (DNO.OL) to buy [USN:L6N45H0B2 TEXT:"Capricorn Energy"] (CNE.L)

item.title: As France erupts, Europe's far right gains from fuel-price anger ahead of elections
item.description: As soaring fuel prices squeeze household budgets and businesses across Europe, cost-of-living pressures are driving unrest and giving fresh momentum to far-right parties.
item.dc:creator: Michel Rose, Angelo Amante, Miranda Murray
item.content:encoded: The tractors rolling into the town of Gela on the southern tip of Europe are flying the Sicilian flag, emblazoned with Medusa, three bent legs and ears of wheat, a reminder of the island's role as a breadbasket since Roman times. But the farmers are not bringing in a harvest. They are protesting. As soaring fuel prices squeeze household budgets and businesses across Europe, cost-of-living pressures are driving unrest and giving fresh momentum to far-right parties ahead of elections next year in countries including France, Italy and Poland. Parties once considered fringe had already been gaining ground, with voters from motorists in rural France to young men in Germany's former Communist east looking for alternatives. The US-Iran war , which erupted in February and sent energy prices sharply higher, has compounded the challenge for governments already struggling to contain inflation, support growth and rein in spending. The discontent has spilled onto the streets. In France, demonstrations that began over deteriorating school facilities in Paris' northern suburbs have morphed into some of the country's worst unrest in decades, with shops looted, buildings torched and a 19th-century town hall in Limoges set on fire. "Why am I here? Well, quite simply, I find the current cost of living truly terrifying," said Quentin Leviloux, a 21-year-old protester in Nantes. "Just think of people who earn barely the minimum wage, when you look at the cost of food, fuel, and everything else. It’s terrifying how incredibly expensive things have become." The European Commission estimates the Iran conflict has cost Europe roughly €100 billion ($112 billion) through disrupted trade and energy markets. Gas prices have jumped about 140% and diesel prices have doubled. In a weekend address, French President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the "legitimate demands" of protesters angered by rising living and fuel costs, while condemning those responsible for violence and looting. "We must never confuse them with those who destroyed, vandalised and looted," he said. PROTESTS ERUPT ACROSS EUROPE Violence has also erupted elsewhere. In the wealthy northern Italian city of Milan, police clashed on Sunday with protesters hurling stones and [USN:L8N4650S6 TEXT:"looting stores"] during demonstrations over poor public services and rising living costs. In Gela, on Sicily's southern coast, farmers say fuel costs have made operating machinery prohibitively expensive. "We cultivate the land, we harvest debts," said one banner. "We are completely at a standstill," said Arcangelo Gambino, a farmers' representative in Caltanissetta province. "The (fuel) cost has more than doubled." Roadblocks by truckers, farmers and steelworkers have disrupted transport across parts of southern Italy, contributing to local fuel shortages and concerns over supermarket supplies. Tens of thousands [USN:L8N46304H TEXT:"marched through Lisbon"] on Saturday over low wages, housing costs and the rising cost of living, increasing pressure on Portugal's centre-right government. In Spain, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home [USN:L1N45U0F8 TEXT:"sparked nationwide demonstrations"] over housing shortages and soaring rents, helping trigger a snap election next month. Belgium has also seen demonstrations, while [USN:L6N464038 TEXT:"large rallies in Albania"] have been driven by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. The protests reflect broader economic anxieties that are increasingly shaping politics across the continent. Concerns about purchasing power have become "a major driver of populist politics" across Europe, said Gilles Ivaldi, a political scientist at Sciences Po. Politicians on both the hard right and hard left have increasingly argued that restoring energy ties with Russia would help lower costs, challenging Europe's mainstream consensus on support for Ukraine. LE PEN MAKES FUEL PRICES A CAMPAIGN ISSUE The latest energy shock comes after years of economic strain following the pandemic and the fallout from Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. In France, rising energy costs have provided an explosive backdrop to next April's presidential election. Macron's government is struggling with a ballooning budget deficit and pressure from bond markets. Frontrunner Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally and hard-left veteran Jean-Luc Melenchon have both made fuel prices central planks in their campaigns. “Rising fuel prices are clearly an issue that boosts Marine Le Pen,” said Ivaldi. “I think this is an issue she has owned for quite some time." Since the Iran war began, [USN:L8N43B0GJ TEXT:"Le Pen's ratings"] have improved while Macron's have slipped, according to polling by Elabe. Le Pen's [USN:L1N45S0C4 TEXT:"proposal to sharply cut"] value-added tax on fuel has attracted broad public support. Analysts say the issue resonates strongly with her core voters in rural and semi-rural areas where car travel is often essential. CALLS TO RESTORE RUSSIA TIES In neighbouring Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading national opinion polls after [USN:L1N45C01D TEXT:"strong gains in local elections"]. The cost of living topped Germans' concerns for a fifth straight year in a survey published this month. [USN:L8N45M0FI TEXT:"German inflation spiked"] to nearly a three-year high in September, with energy price inflation rising to 14.9%, handing ammunition to the AfD to [USN:L6N45D0RG TEXT:"attack Chancellor Friedrich Merz"]. The AfD is pushing to [USN:L8N4591QO TEXT:"restore energy ties"] with Russia, arguing that Berlin’s support for Ukraine is needlessly self-sabotaging at a time when Europe’s largest economy and many of its energy-hungry companies are struggling. Past experience indicates a link between high energy prices and voter turnout for the AfD, said Jan Steckel, professor for the political economy of climate change at the Technical University of Munich. “Populist parties often frame energy costs as avoidable and attribute them to government policy choices ... rather than to the underlying geopolitical shocks that drive them," he said. “These geopolitical shocks are ... much more difficult to explain. And I think this is why incumbent parties often struggle." The argument is gaining traction elsewhere. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces growing competition from National Future, a new far-right party led by former army general Roberto Vannacci that advocates restoring gas links with Russia. In Poland, one of Ukraine's staunchest supporters, concern over energy bills is helping boost support for the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown. Its leader, Grzegorz Braun, has called for a return to buying Russian oil and gas, making the case alongside AfD politicians in Lubmin, where the damaged Nord Stream pipelines land in Germany. “I love the smell of Russian gas in the morning,” he said. ($1 = 0.8921 euros)

item.title: Markets' squeal is music to Fed ears — but still too faint
item.description: If Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is happy to let financial markets do some of the central bank's work, he should be pleased with the recent selloff in stocks and bonds. But the recent tightening in financial conditions is far from enough to let him off the hook.
item.dc:creator: Mike Dolan
item.content:encoded: If Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is happy to let financial markets do some of the central bank's work, he should be pleased with the recent [USN:L8N4620KK TEXT:"selloff in stocks and bonds"]. But the recent tightening in financial conditions is far from enough to let him off the hook. The new Fed boss has repeatedly made clear that overall access to finance shows little sign of being restricted by the central bank, despite an economy that has [USN:S0N40K04F TEXT:"proven resilient"] and continues to generate uncomfortably fast price growth. In his keynote speech at the Jackson Hole conference in August — a speech that clearly flagged the Fed's first interest rate rise in three years last month — Warsh detailed aspects of lending, credit and market behaviour that suggested prevailing Fed policy was simply not tight enough. "On balance, I would be hard-pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive," he said then. The question for investors is whether that's still the case, and whether higher bond yields, wider credit spreads and stock-market volatility since August have tightened financial conditions enough to keep the Fed at bay. The answer seems to be "not yet". But a cat-and-mouse game between markets and Fed expectations may now play out over what could be a bumpy year-end. CONDITIONAL The Chicago Fed's National Financial Conditions Index (NFCI) is one place to see the overall impact of recent market turbulence. By the end of last week, it had risen to the tightest level since April, while the Goldman Sachs equivalent had hit its tightest since March. That shows the greater difficulty in raising debt or equity since the Fed hiked rates and catapulted expectations for further rate rises higher over the coming year. Underlying price shifts since Warsh's Jackson Hole appearance show where that's been felt most. Even though it is well off its recent 24-year peak, the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield is still up almost 50 basis points over the intervening two months. Thirty-year fixed mortgage rates are up 70 bps and US junk bond risk spreads (.MERH0A0) have widened by almost 100 bps. Reflecting the mortgage squeeze, housebuilding sentiment as measured by the National Association of Home Builders fell this month to its lowest level in 14-1/2 years. Crude oil futures are up more than 20% over the past two months and the dollar (.DXY) is up almost 3%. Buoyant stock indexes, riding the AI boom, had offset edgier credit and debt markets for the past year or more — until last week. But that's no longer happening, with the S&P 500 (.SPX) and tech-heavy Nasdaq (.IXIC) basically unchanged since Jackson Hole. Just as significantly for financial conditions, equity volatility embodied by the VIX "fear index" (.VIX) has started to stir too, signalling danger ahead and increased risk for initial public offerings and equity financing. It hit its highest level in four months on Friday. The bond market equivalent (.MOVE) , often important for finance via securities repurchase, or repo, markets, has also surged back to March levels since August. Higher equity values intuitively loosen financial conditions via wealth effects, and vice versa, but the way the Chicago Fed's NFCI is compiled shows where the real pressure points lie. The index is broken down into three categories: risk, credit and leverage. The VIX is a component of the risk subsection, higher-risk credit is often correlated with equities, and leverage readings hinge on debt-to-equity ratios that are highly sensitive to equity prices. The threat of a blowup at the epicentre of the highly leveraged AI buildout, as seen with [USN:L4N461208 TEXT:"CoreWeave"] (CRWV.O) last week, could ripple through wider financing conditions and indexes that capture them quite quickly. That helps explain why the bond market, while absorbing two worrying [USN:L1N460127 TEXT:"inflation reports"] last week, rallied hard on signs that the AI rally underpinning stock benchmarks may be about to roll over. However, the tipping point seems some way off. Even though the Chicago Fed index is at its tightest since April, it remains well below its 20-year average and has remained on the loose side for the best part of three years. EVEN WORSE? But there are other readings on financial conditions that suggest the recent tightening may be more extreme. Morgan Stanley's equity strategist Mike Wilson and team said on Monday that their financial conditions index (FCI), a compilation of rates, the dollar and energy prices, was at its tightest since 2022. They also noted that economically sensitive stocks have lost nearly 10% since August. "Some acknowledgement of this tightening by Warsh would be well received by rate-sensitive areas that have already de-rated notably," they said. As for Warsh, he's now in a blackout period along with his Fed colleagues until next week's policy meeting, and there appears to be a consensus that the next rate rise will not come until [USN:L4N3XG141 TEXT:"December"]. But some saw his comments at the [USN:S0N40K04F TEXT:"International Monetary Fund meeting"] last week in Bangkok as indicating that he still didn't think the Fed had yet done all it needed to do to rein in inflation. In describing the Fed's September hike, Warsh said, "We removed a dose of accommodation" — clearly not all of the accommodation, suggesting he still thinks conditions are too loose. If the Fed does skip a rate rise next week, just six days before the midterm elections , it would probably take a significant further jolt in financial conditions over the following six weeks for policymakers to stay their hand at year-end.
